title: He Dug His Father's Wells Again — Famine, a Lie, a Well
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Of the fifty chapters of Genesis, exactly one is given over from beginning to end to Isaac's own affairs. Everywhere else in the book he turns up either as Abraham's son or as Jacob's father.

And this chapter reads with a strange sense of familiarity — because every single thing in it is something his father did first. A famine. Calling his wife his sister. Quarrelling with Abimelech over wells. Cutting a covenant. Building an altar. The author has written it this way on purpose.
So the question this lesson puts to you is this: is there a pattern in your family that has been handed down and handed down, and that you hope will stop in your generation?
It might be rage. It might be the silent treatment. It might be a refusal ever to admit fault. It might be measuring love in money. It might be drink.

Let me put the answer up front: a weakness left unhandled gets passed on to the next generation — but a well that has been filled in can be dug open again. And a man who knows whose land it is does not have to fight to the death over one well.
1. The Same Famine, a Different Command
Verse 1: "There was a famine in the land, in addition to the first famine that was in the days of Abraham. Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines, to Gerar."
Brothers and sisters, the author goes out of his way to mention his father's famine. He wants you to hold the two of them up side by side.
And verse 2: "Yahweh appeared to him, and said, 'Don't go down into Egypt.'"
"Go down into Egypt" — אַל־תֵּרֵד מִצְרָיְמָה — and that verb is precisely the one used in 12:10, "Abram went down into Egypt."
The same famine. The father went down; the son is expressly stopped.

Brothers and sisters, this matters enormously for us: what a spiritual elder did cannot automatically become your guidance. In the very same situation, God gives different people different words. Principles carry across; specific guidance cannot simply be copied.

In pastoral work I hear one sentence again and again: "Well, Pastor So-and-so did it this way back then." Sometimes that sentence is wisdom. Sometimes it is laziness — because it spares a person the labour of asking God for himself.
And once God has stopped him, what does he say? Verses 3 to 5: "I will be with you, and will bless you … and I will establish the oath which I swore to Abraham your father."

"I will be with you" — וְאֶהְיֶה עִמְּךָ. Notice that verb: it is the very root standing behind Exodus 3:14, "I AM WHO I AM." What God gives Isaac is not a new promise. It is the renewal of his father's one promise.
And verse 5 is more interesting still: "because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my requirements, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws."
Brothers and sisters, Sinai is still four hundred years away, and God is already using four words out of the law to describe the whole of one man's life.
Both of them faced a famine. Why did God let Abraham go down to Egypt and forbid Isaac?

Strictly speaking, God never did "let" Abraham go down to Egypt. Chapter 12 simply records that he went — and what followed was a string of troubles. By chapter 26, God steps in of his own accord: "Don't go down into Egypt. Live in the land I will tell you about." So the difference between the two is not a matter of rules. It is a matter of God's guidance for this particular man at this particular moment. That is intensely practical for us: what somebody else may do is not necessarily what you may do, and the same action in a different season may get a different answer. So do not use "but so-and-so did it too" as your reason — ask God yourself. And do not use your own guidance to bind another person's conscience.
"Live in this land" sounds very passive. What kind of command is that?

In a famine, staying put is a great deal harder than leaving. And what God gives is not passive waiting — he adds a sentence, "I will be with you, and will bless you," and he restates the covenant made with Abraham. Then verse 12 says, "Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted." To sow in famine-struck ground is itself an act of faith. So the content of "live in this land" is this: stay where God has told you to stay, do the work that needs doing, and then watch how God blesses. The reminder for us is plain. When you are held in a place that looks as though it has no future, the thing to do is not to engineer a way out. It is to ask first whether there is a field here you could sow.
2. The Same Lie, a Third Time
Verse 7: "The men of the place asked him about his wife. He said, 'She is my sister.'"

Brothers and sisters, this is the third time that sentence appears in Genesis. Genesis 12:13, in Egypt. Genesis 20:2, in Gerar. And now 26:7, in Gerar again. The father said it twice; the son has now said it once.
The same sentence, the same city, even the same royal name.
And Isaac's reasoning is his father's, word for word: "lest, he thought, 'the men of the place might kill me for Rebekah, because she is beautiful to look at.'"
His father had said, "Because I thought, 'Surely the fear of God is not in this place.'"

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed something? By the time Isaac was born, all of that was over. He never watched his father tell that lie with his own eyes — when chapter 20 happened, he had not yet been born.
So how did he learn it?

There are two possibilities. One is that he had heard the family stories. The other is more common still — he did not learn it, he inherited it. That reflex, the one that says "when pressure comes, protect yourself first," never has to be taught. It travels down through the atmosphere of a house.
I have seen it far too often in pastoral work: a man who swore from childhood, "I will never turn into my father," and who at forty is speaking to his own child in exactly his father's tone of voice.

And this chapter's ending is every bit as humiliating as the two before it. Abimelech looked out of a window and saw Isaac caressing Rebekah his wife, and he called him in and said, "Behold, surely she is your wife. Why did you say, 'She is my sister'?"
Once again a pagan king is rebuking a man who carries God's promise. Three times in a row.
Isaac calls his wife his sister as well — that makes three. Why does the Bible bother to record a repetition like this?

Because it is true to life: the faults of a family are hereditary. Abraham said it twice, Isaac said it a third time — and Isaac was not even present for either of his father's episodes. He either heard about it, or it simply grew in him. That matters a great deal for us, because children do not learn what we teach them; they learn what we do. And some reflexes skip a generation and come back in a different shape. The practical step is this: say out loud, and write down, the pattern that keeps recurring in your family, and then, in your generation, make one deliberate choice in the opposite direction. That is exactly the heart of this lesson — the line is meant to stop with you.
Why is it Abimelech, a pagan king, who rebukes Isaac, and not God?

Verse 10: "Abimelech said, 'What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt on us!'" Again and again Scripture lets outsiders rebuke the people of God — and that is a severe way to write. What it is saying is that God's children may never assume they stand on higher moral ground than everyone else. And what deserves even more attention is what Abimelech does next: he issues an order — "He who touches this man or his wife will surely be put to death" — he protects them by means of an institution. So sometimes God is protecting his people through people who do not believe in him, and through structures of law.
3. A Light from the Original: Dug Open Again, One Well at a Time
From verse 12 on, we come to the most beautiful part of this chapter.
"Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him. The man grew great, and grew more and more until he became very great."

Brothers and sisters, notice where that sentence stands — immediately after the lie. The text does not say, "because he got it right, he was blessed." It says, "Yahweh blessed him." That is God's faithfulness, not Isaac's technique.
Then verses 14 and 15: "The Philistines envied him. Now all the wells which his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped, and filled with earth."
And verse 18 is the pivot of the whole chapter:

"Isaac dug again the wells of water, which they had dug in the days of Abraham his father, for the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham. He called their names after the names by which his father had called them."
Brothers and sisters, there are two actions in that one verse, and each of them deserves a stop.
The first action is "dug again." Those wells were already there; they had simply been filled in with earth. He did not have to go and find a new water source. All he had to do was clear the dirt out.

And that is the most accurate picture of revival there is. Revival is usually not the digging of a new well; it is clearing the earth out of an old one. Isaiah 58:12 says, "Those who will be of you will build the old waste places. You will raise up the foundations of many generations."
The second action is harder: "He called their names after the names by which his father had called them."

Brothers and sisters, he could perfectly well have given them new names. He dug them; the labour was his, the risk was his. And in that world, naming a well after yourself was the accepted way of declaring ownership.
He called back the names his father had given, without altering a single word.
That is an extraordinarily mature act. Maturity in a successor shows itself as a refusal to hurry and stamp his own seal on things.

And here I want to point out an observation that goes straight to the heart: a spiritual inheritance does not pass down by itself. Every generation has to dig it out again — the well the last generation dug, this generation has to clear with its own hands. But if the man doing the digging is busy changing the names and putting up his own signboard, that well becomes his own monument, and not his father's well.
"He dug his father's wells again" — does that mean faith is just a matter of walking the way the previous generation walked?

Not copying — receiving. The text says the Philistines "had stopped them after the death of Abraham," and that Isaac "called their names after the names by which his father had called them." He recognised the line he stood in, and he kept the names. But he was not only repairing old things: in verse 22 he digs a new well and calls it Rehoboth, saying, "For now Yahweh has made room for us." So the healthy picture is both together — dig out again what was genuine in the previous generation, and also dig the new well that belongs to yours. Keep only the old and it dries up; chase only the new and the roots are cut.
4. Yielding All the Way to the Third Well
Verses 19 to 22 are a very quiet stretch of narrative, and a very powerful one.

"Isaac's servants dug in the valley, and found there a well of flowing water. The herdsmen of Gerar argued with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, 'The water is ours.' So he called the name of the well Esek, because they contended with him."
"They dug another well, and they argued over that, also. So he called its name Sitnah."
Sitnah, שִׂטְנָה, means "hostility, accusation" — and the root of that word is the very word behind the name Satan.
"He left that place, and dug another well. They didn't argue over that one. So he called it Rehoboth. He said, 'For now Yahweh has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.'"
Brothers and sisters: the first well was seized, the second well was seized, and over the third one nobody came to argue.
And his response was the same every time: leave that place, and dig another.
It is easy to preach this as weakness, but listen to what he actually says: "For now Yahweh has made room for us." He knew that what gave him room was not the well. It was Yahweh.

He was not a man without a line — in verse 27 he says to Abimelech's face, "Why have you come to me, since you hate me, and have sent me away from you?" He said his piece plainly, and only then did he cut a covenant.
Over possessions you may yield; over what is right you must speak. That is the finest thing he received from his father.
And in verse 28, the reason those men give for coming to make a covenant is this: "We saw plainly that Yahweh was with you."
Brothers and sisters, the men who said that are the very men who took his wells.
If you keep yielding after two wells have been taken from you, won't you just be trampled on for good?

Isaac yielded twice, and over the third well nobody argued. The text does not say this is the only way to act, and it does not make a rule of it — Scripture elsewhere records people who stood their ground and argued their case; Paul appealed to Caesar. What this passage wants us to see is the ground he stood on: he could afford to yield because he knew the land and the water were God's to give. So the question to discern is not "should I contend or not?" but "whichever I do, what is holding me up while I do it?" And one practical word has to be added here: if it is somebody else's rights that are being violated, or if unlawfulness or safety is involved, then endless yielding is not the answer, and the matter should be handled through the proper channels.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "digging his father's wells again" as conservatism, as a refusal to be renewed. What Isaac dug was a well of flowing water; he was not curating antiques. The point is the water source, not the shape of the stonework. Preach it as conservatism and your congregation will start using tradition to block the work of the Holy Spirit. Here is the test: when they have heard you, do they go back to the source, or do they clutch the form?

The second is preaching "do not contend" as though nothing may ever be contended for. In verse 27 he speaks perfectly bluntly. Over possessions you may yield; over what is right you must speak. Without that distinction you will raise a congregation who dare not face a problem, and who have learned to call their avoidance humility.

The third is preaching the hundredfold harvest as proof that believing makes you rich. That verse comes immediately after the lie, and what the text is stressing is God's faithfulness, not Isaac's method. Preach it as a formula and the brothers and sisters in the room who are not earning much will walk out convinced they are not blessed — and that is a very deep wound to inflict.

The fourth is preaching only Isaac's weakness and never what he carried on. That run of well-digging in verses 18 to 22 is the finest stretch of his whole life. If your entire message is about the lie, this chapter turns into a scolding. What the congregation ought to carry home is those wells with the water coming up in them again.

The fifth is preaching Isaac as a lightweight, a transitional figure with no spiritual weight of his own. People call him "bland", they say he "has no story", and there is contempt in the tone of it. But look at verse 24: what God says to him is every bit as weighty as what he said to Abraham — "I am the God of Abraham your father. Don't be afraid, for I am with you." The assignment of the second generation is not pioneering; it is keeping what was handed over. And keeping is no easier than pioneering.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: there is a very bad pattern in my family, and from childhood I swore I would never become like that — but I am finding I look more and more like it. What do I do? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives us three directions. First, admit that it is real. In the passage where Isaac lies, Scripture does not cover for him and does not supply him with excuses. Admitting that a pattern exists is the first step towards breaking it; a great many people are stuck precisely because they are still busy proving "I'm not that much like him." Second, you need one sentence God has spoken to you himself. In verse 2 God says to Isaac, "Don't go down into Egypt" — a sentence his father never received. What you need is not stronger willpower. It is one sentence you are certain God has said to you, and then one occasion on which you act on it. Third, find people to do it with you. Isaac had servants digging the wells alongside him. A pattern like this is very hard to break on your own; you need a spiritual companion, somebody who can flag it for you at the moment your old reflex appears.

The second question: the older people in our church hold hard to the old ways, the young want to change things, and both sides are getting hurt — what help is there in this chapter? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives us a remarkably balanced picture. First, what Isaac dug was a well of flowing water — what he wanted was water, not a particular style of well. So the question for the young is this: is it the form we want to change, or the water source? If it is the form, that can be talked through. If we want to swap out the water source itself, that is another matter altogether. Second, he "called their names after the names by which his father had called them." That is the lesson for the younger generation: you may do new things, but you need not hurry to prove that they are yours. Changing a name takes a moment. Carrying a name on takes a long time. Third, the older generation has homework too: those wells were filled in by the Philistines, not by Isaac. The real enemy is not the next generation who want to dig; it is the earth that choked the wells — rigidity, injury, old accounts never settled. If the elders will get down and clear the earth alongside the young, then that well belongs to two generations at once.
Can a problem that has repeated generation after generation in a family really stop with me?

It can — but the method has to be right. First, see it and call it by name — not by blaming your elders, but by describing the pattern honestly (for example, "in our family, when there is conflict we go silent"). Second, work out what it gives you: any pattern that survives three generations survives because it works in the short term, and you need to know what you are getting out of it. Third, practise one action in the opposite direction, and make it small and concrete. Fourth, find someone to walk with you, because when pressure comes people revert to factory settings. And if that pattern involves violence, addiction or long-term harm, please do seek pastoral and professional help — do not rely on resolve alone.
7. Living 321 Out — Carry It On, Without Rushing to Set Up Your Own House
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — twice a well was taken from Isaac and he did not fight for it. And 1 Peter 2:23 says of the Lord Jesus, "When he was cursed, he didn't curse back. When he suffered, he didn't threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously." Brothers and sisters, here is my role model: he could have contended, and he chose to yield, because he knew his portion was held with the Father. The weight of that sentence is in its second half — not because he was weak, but because he was sure.

The Bible is my standard — look at those four words in verse 5: requirements, commandments, statutes, laws. Four hundred years before Sinai, God is already describing one man's life in the language of the law. A standard does not begin the day the clauses are written down; it has been at work inside the relationship all along.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — in verse 2 God says, "Don't go down into Egypt." Brothers and sisters, being stopped is God speaking. We are so used to counting only the opened door as guidance and treating the closed door as a setback. But in this chapter, the most important guidance God gives Isaac is a "do not".

Let Jesus be King — accept the door that has closed, and stop shoving at it. Isaac did not go down to Egypt; he stayed in a famine-struck place and sowed, and it was there that God gave him a hundredfold harvest. Brothers and sisters, the place where you feel trapped right now may be precisely the place God has told you to stay.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — in verse 28, the men who had seized his wells say, "We saw plainly that Yahweh was with you." Sometimes the way glory goes to God is not by our declaring it, but by somebody else's observation. And the most powerful testimony very often comes out of the mouth of the person who once wronged you.

Establish God's system — he dug his father's wells again, and kept his father's names on them. Brothers and sisters, revival is very often not the digging of a new well but the clearing of the earth out of an old one. To establish God's system you have to be willing to carry something on, rather than hurrying off to set up a house of your own. And that takes a very rare kind of character: to do the work, and not want the name.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We talk a great deal about handing things on, about spiritual parents and spiritual children, about passing this line down. This chapter reminds us of two things. First, an inheritance carries the weaknesses along with it. If you do not deal with your own old reflexes, your spiritual children will pick them up — and they may not pick them up by learning, but by infection. Second, the one who takes the baton has both the right and the duty to dig it out again. The previous generation's experience does not automatically become the next generation's experience; every generation has to clear the earth with its own hands and taste the water of that well for itself. So do not lose patience when a young person "asks again a question we settled years ago" — that is exactly what digging a well looks like.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Well Choked With Earth
Brothers and sisters, one and the same well, choked with earth, is seen quite differently by four different hearts.

The proud heart says, "The last generation did a poor job of it; I am going to start over." The moment this heart takes charge it wants to change the names, replace the structures, run up its own flag. Brothers and sisters, look at what Isaac did: he dug the same well, and he used the same name. Truly taking the baton is not overturning. It is clearing earth.

The fearful heart says, "They keep taking the wells — am I supposed to dig again?" This heart is turned down twice and does not dare open its mouth a third time. To a heart like that I want to say: Isaac did not stop until the third well. And the name of that third well is "room". If your first and your second have been seized, will you dig a third? God's wide open space is very often at the third well.

The ashamed heart says, "I have done it again — the very thing my father did." You may only have discovered lately that you have reproduced the pattern you most despise. Brothers and sisters, look at the architecture of this chapter: the lie is in verse 7, and the wells come after verse 18. The text does not stop at his failure. It goes straight on to record the finest stretch of his whole life. Your weakness today is not the last verse of your chapter.

The wounded heart says, "I keep yielding, and I keep being robbed." You may be the one at home who always gives way, or the one on the team who is always taken advantage of. Brothers and sisters, I want to say two things here, and to say them carefully. First, Isaac's yielding was yielding with solid ground underneath it — he knew the land was God's. If your yielding comes out of fear, then the thing that needs healing is the fear, not one more round of giving way. Second, look at verse 27: in the end he said his piece plainly. To yield is not the same thing as never speaking.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, identify one family pattern. Write down one thing your parents did that you do not want to go on doing. Write it down, and then pray over it once. Naming it is the first step towards breaking it.

Second, clear the earth off one well. Find one good thing the previous generation left behind that now lies abandoned — a family altar, a custom kept at a festival, an older relative's testimony of faith — and this week, restore it once.

Third, do one thing without signing your name to it. Do the work, and let somebody else's name stay on it. This is the hardest exercise in the chapter, and the one that shows most clearly whether you are really taking the baton.
Fourth, dig the third well. If there is something you have already been refused twice, try once more this week. It was not until the third well that Isaac could call it "room".

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences: there is a man in the Bible whose father's wells had all been stopped up with earth, and he dug them out again one by one; what surprised me most is that when he had finished, he still used his father's names for them, without changing a single word; and later even the men who had seized his wells came and said to him, we saw plainly that God is with you.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that a weakness left unhandled is passed on to the next generation, and that in my generation I will bring it to a stop.
I declare that I will dig open again the wells that were filled in, rather than hurrying off to sink new ones.
I declare that I do my work without needing my name on it; I am willing to use the name the last generation gave.
I declare that what gives me room is not the well; it is Yahweh.
I am supposed to "dig one well open again" this week, and I do not know which well to dig.

Look in three places. First, a spiritual habit you once had and that life has since silted up: a fixed time in Scripture, grace before meals, preparing for Sunday. Second, a tradition your household once kept and then let drop: eating together, praying together, speaking a blessing at the turn of the year. Third, a relationship that has been stopped up: that person you were once close to and then simply stopped contacting. Pick one, and dig it open this week — you do not have to dig it all the way down; one spadeful is enough. And do it Isaac's way, keeping the name: tell your family, "this is something our family used to do, and I want to pick it back up."
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be a man crouched beside a well that has been filled in, lifting the earth out of it one spadeful at a time.
His father dug those wells. Other people put the earth in. And the work of clearing it out could only be done by him.
He dug for a long while, and at last the water came up. And then he did something nobody had asked him to do — he called back his father's names for them, without altering a single word.
Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: is there a well like that in your hands?

It might be the faith your parents had when they were young, since choked by the weight of making a living. It might be your church's prayer meeting of twenty years ago, since choked by procedure and by tiredness. It might be that simple fire you yourself had ten years back, buried by disappointment one spadeful at a time.
That well is still there. The water source has not changed; it has only been covered over with earth.
And the work of clearing the earth wins no applause, and nobody will do it in your place.
But remember verse 22: when he had dug the third well he said, "For now Yahweh has made room for us."
And remember verse 24, where God appeared to him that same night, and the first thing he said was, "Don't be afraid, for I am with you."

The focus is not on whether I resemble my parents, not on how many wells have been taken from me, and not on whether anybody remembers who did the digging. The focus is on Jesus — he is the one who said to the Samaritan woman, "the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life." Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to name one pattern that is to stop, and to put our hands to clearing the earth off one well. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the ordinary days. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ In a famine, "live in this land" is harder than leaving. What is actually inside that command?
2. ★★★ The same lie has now reached a third generation. What does that tell us about what children actually learn?
3. ★ Once again a pagan king rebukes the people of God. Why does Scripture keep writing it that way?
4. ★★ Isaac both dug the old wells again and dug a new one. What becomes of those who only keep the old? And of those who only chase the new?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I am nothing like my parents), fearful (when I feel unsafe I protect myself first), ashamed (I am finding I look more and more like him), wounded (I am the one that pattern was inflicted on). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Don't be afraid, for I am with you, and will bless you." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a pattern that keeps recurring in your family? What short-term benefit did it give you all, such that it could go on being handed down?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "The thing I least want to turn into is …"
9. ★★ This week, in which particular situation will you make one move in the opposite direction? Say it small, and say it concretely.

Leader's reminder: when family patterns are discussed, do not let it turn into a meeting for criticising parents. The group leader should steer each person to speak only about his own share. If violence, addiction or long-term harm is involved, follow up privately after the meeting and help them find professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own household, which well has been stopped up — a tradition you once had and then let drop? How will you dig it open this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your area of service, which good old practice ought to be picked back up?
12. ★★★ The digging-a-new-well exercise: this week, alongside picking up something old, begin one new habit that belongs to your own generation. Say what it is and when you will do it.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the family pattern you mean to stop, and ask him to flag it for you when you revert to factory settings. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: in the Bible the same lie was told twice by a father, and then once again by his son. Second: what that son later did was to dig his father's stopped-up wells open again, one at a time. Third: so I have been asking myself which line I want to stop, and which well I want to dig back open. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the well you will dig open this week, and the one opposite move you will make. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to bring that wounding line to a stop in our generation.
